fixes.explanation: Balak, king of Moab, goes out to meet Balaam at the border (Numbers 22:36). Then he opens with, “Did I not send you an urgent summons? Why did you not come to me?” (Numbers 22:37). He asks about the delay before anything else. No small talk at all. My mustache would've at least tried a hello.

No thank-you here. Balak opens with, “Did I not send you an urgent summons?” (Numbers 22:37). That's a question about why Balaam didn't come sooner, not a thank-you. I think a welcome basket was never part of the king's plan.

The next morning Balak brings Balaam up to Bamoth-baal, and “…he could see the outskirts of the camp of the people.” (Numbers 22:41). That's what the text gives for the view. Think of spotting my bakery's front step from a hill.

The text never mentions the land of Canaan from up there. It says Balaam “…could see the outskirts of the camp of the people.” (Numbers 22:41). That's the view from Bamoth-baal. A whole land would be a huge view, and the text keeps it to the camp's outskirts.

The text says the opposite. Balaam asks for seven altars (Numbers 23:1), and in the very next verse Balak does just what Balaam asked. No argument is recorded. Then Balak and Balaam offer a bull and a ram on each altar (Numbers 23:2).

Right, and here's what the text says. Balaam asks for seven altars, and Balak does just what he asked. Then he and Balaam offer a bull and a ram on each altar (Numbers 23:2). The text records no pushback at all. Tell my mustache to pack seven cookie boxes and I'd get at least one sigh.

The text says nothing about Israel's camp moving. Balaam's hope is about the LORD: “Perhaps the LORD will meet with me.” (Numbers 23:3). That's why he heads off to a barren height. His words there are about a meeting with God, not about the camp.

Yes, a message. The text says the LORD “…put a message in Balaam’s mouth…” (Numbers 23:5). Then Balaam is told, “Return to Balak and give him this message.” He carries what he was given. I know what it's like to deliver a box exactly as packed.

A curse is what Balak asked for, and Balaam repeats that request in his oracle (Numbers 23:7). But the text says the LORD put a message in Balaam's mouth and sent him back to Balak (Numbers 23:5). So what Balak asked for and what the LORD gave are two different things.

No riddles here. The word in the text is a message, and the LORD tells Balaam, “Return to Balak and give him this message.” (Numbers 23:5). Balaam is sent to hand it over, like a box with the address already on it. Nothing in the verse calls it a puzzle.

It's God. Balaam asks, “How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?” (Numbers 23:8). His question rests on what God has done. The next line asks the same thing with the LORD's name: “How can I denounce those whom the LORD has not denounced?”

Moab is where Balak is king, so I get why it jumps out. But Moab is on the asking side, not the one who has not cursed Israel. Balaam says, “How can I curse those whom God has not cursed?” (Numbers 23:8). I once grabbed my rolling pin when I needed my stamper, just because it was nearby. Same kind of mix-up.
Balak never says warned. His complaint is, “…you have only blessed them!” (Numbers 23:11). He asked for a curse and got a blessing. I bet that stung.

Carmel isn't named in this passage. The text says Balak took Balaam “…to the field of Zophim, to the top of Pisgah…” (Numbers 23:14). Balak is changing the scenery, so it's easy to blur the mountains together. Pisgah is the one this passage names.

That question belonged to the border, when Balak said, “Why did you not come to me?” (Numbers 22:37). This time Balak asks, “What did the LORD say?” (Numbers 23:17). It's a different question for a different moment. I bet the message is on his mind more than the clock.

Balaam gives no expiration date. He says, “He has blessed, and I cannot change it.” (Numbers 23:20). Just before that he asks, “Does He promise and not fulfill?” (Numbers 23:19). A year is a number he never mentions. I set a timer for everything in my bakery, but Balaam never brings one up.

Babylon isn't in Balaam's words here. He says, “God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox.” (Numbers 23:22). Babylon is a famous name, so it's tempting, like reaching for the fanciest cookie cutter first. The place Balaam names is Egypt.

Assyria doesn't appear in this passage. Balaam says, “God brought them out of Egypt with strength like a wild ox.” (Numbers 23:22). The place he names is Egypt. I've reached for the next shelf over in my bakery plenty of times, so I get the mix-up.

The text says the opposite. Balaam says, “For there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel.” (Numbers 23:23). So no spell works against Israel, and no divination does either. There's no right one hiding in the pile.

That's how Balaam's picture goes: “…not resting until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain.” (Numbers 23:24). The picture is of a people who rise like a lioness and rouse themselves like a lion. They don't rest until those things happen. It's a heavy image, and Balaam leaves it just as it is.

Balaam gives no time of day. He says the people do not rest “…until they devour their prey and drink the blood of the slain.” (Numbers 23:24). Those actions are what the picture names, not the sunset. So the not resting runs until those things happen in the picture.

True. Balak says, “Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!” (Numbers 23:25). He started out asking for a curse (Numbers 23:13), and now he asks for neither one. I think two blessings in a row changed his order.

Balak's words are, “Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there.” (Numbers 23:27). His hope is about a curse from a new place, not about the camp. Nothing in the text has Israel moving anywhere. It's like checking the same oven again and hoping the timer reads different this time.
The text says Peor “…overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). That's what the top of Peor looks over. Balak brings Balaam up there for the third spot. Wasteland is the word to hang onto.

The Jordan River isn't mentioned in this passage. The text says Peor “…overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). It's easy to picture a river down there. But the text names the wasteland, and that's the view from the top of Peor.

The Salt Sea isn't named in this passage. The text says Peor “…overlooks the wasteland.” (Numbers 23:28). A sea sounds like a nicer view, I'll admit. But the text gives the wasteland, and that's what Balak's third spot overlooks.
